text_blocks.snippet: The IRS calculates age 59 1/2 by determining when someone reaches the six-month anniversary of their 59th birthday. For example, if your birthday is June 1st, you would be considered 59 1/2 on December 1st. This rule is in place to deter early withdrawals from retirement accounts, as withdrawals before this age often incur a 10% penalty.

list.title: The Core Concept:
list.snippet: The IRS doesn't calculate "half-years" in the traditional sense. Instead, they use the six-month anniversary of a person's 59th birthday as the point when they are considered 59 1/2.

list.title: Example:
list.snippet: If your 59th birthday is on June 1, 2025, you would turn 59 1/2 on December 1, 2025.

list.title: Early Withdrawal Penalties:
list.snippet: The primary reason for this rule is to discourage individuals from withdrawing from retirement accounts (like 401(k)s and IRAs) before the age of 59 1/2. Such withdrawals are typically subject to a 10% penalty in addition to regular income tax.

list.title: Exceptions:
list.snippet: There are exceptions to this rule, such as withdrawals made after the age of 55 from a 401(k) if the individual has separated from service, or withdrawals for specific purposes like first-time home purchases, disability, or higher education expenses.

list.title: Tax Implications:
list.snippet: It's important to consult with a financial advisor or tax professional for guidance on specific situations, especially when considering early withdrawals from retirement accounts.
